hints: Focus on what each test actually proves, and ask yourself whether it narrows T down to one group or leaves several possibilities open.
Complete combustion to only $\text{CO}_2$ and $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ tells you T contains carbon and hydrogen, but it may also contain oxygen.
Steamy fumes with $\text{PCl}_5$ show an $\text{-OH}$ group is present, while no precipitate with 2,4-DNPH rules out the carbonyls that do react.
walkthrough:
**Use the combustion result**

Think simply first. Making only carbon dioxide and water means T must contain C and H.

$$\text{T} + \text{O}_2 \rightarrow \text{CO}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$ 
But oxygen could also be present in T, because oxygen in the fuel does not give a new combustion product. So T could be a hydrocarbon or an oxygen-containing organic compound.

**Use the PCl5 result**

Steamy fumes are $\text{HCl}$ gas. This is the classic positive test for a compound containing an $\text{-OH}$ group.

$$\text{R-OH} + \text{PCl}_5 \rightarrow \text{R-Cl} + \text{POCl}_3 + \text{HCl}$$ 
So T contains $\text{-OH}$. That fits an alcohol, a carboxylic acid, or a phenol. It rules out a hydrocarbon, which has no $\text{-OH}$ to react.

**Use the 2,4-DNPH result**

2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazine gives an orange-yellow precipitate with aldehydes and ketones, the carbonyl compounds with $\text{C=O}$.

No visible product means no aldehyde and no ketone reaction has happened. So T cannot be an aldehyde.

**Ask what is certain**

We know T has $\text{-OH}$ and is not a carbonyl, but we cannot tell which $\text{-OH}$ type it is from this data alone. Alcohol and carboxylic acid both fit.

Therefore the only statement we can make with complete certainty is the negative one, that T is not an aldehyde.

options.A: A carboxylic acid would fit the results, it has $\text{-OH}$ for $\text{PCl}_5$ and no 2,4-DNPH reaction, but an alcohol would also fit. We cannot be certain it is specifically a carboxylic acid.
options.B: A hydrocarbon contains only C and H. It has no $\text{-OH}$ group, so it would not give steamy fumes of $\text{HCl}$ with $\text{PCl}_5$. This option is contradicted by the evidence.
options.C: An alcohol would fit the results, but so would a carboxylic acid. Both contain $\text{-OH}$ and both are negative with 2,4-DNPH. We cannot be certain it is specifically an alcohol.
options.D: All aldehydes give a visible orange precipitate with 2,4-DNPH reagent. Since T gives no visible product, T definitely cannot be an aldehyde. This is the only conclusion that follows with certainty.
